component.name: rhYciv
component.summary: A crisp, high-resolution turn-based empire strategy game

description.p: rhYciv is a classic turn-based empire strategy game with a modern high-resolution renderer, deeper zoom, streamlined conquest rules, and attributed open-source artwork.
The bundled rules, interface data, fonts, and art make this a standalone game; no commercial game installation is required.

The bugs 0.2.0 shipped, found by playing it. Capturing a city in a loaded game no longer takes the game down. Goody huts stay taken, rivers join up and widen from a trickle to an estuary, the sea has water in it again and the coast meets the grass. A long press sends a unit where you point it, zooming keeps the unit you were moving, and a Diplomat can buy an empty city instead of destroying it. Barbarians no longer declare war, and nobody you have never met offers you peace.

Diplomacy is an audience you stay in, with the other leader in view throughout: forty-two portraits, one for each civilisation in each gender. Imported Civilization II games keep their wonders, which had been read from the save and discarded, taking a city's happiness with them. Trade routes are paid Civilization II's rate rather than Civilization I's, a city square always yields at least one shield, and the terrain specials table has been checked entry by entry against the original's own Civilopedia.
The hard crashes, and the first release checked against the original.

Sessions had been ending in a crash with no managed exception and nothing on standard error since 0.1.6. The output capture added in 0.1.8 caught it, and it was arithmetic rather than a fault: one afternoon's play loaded 4,170 GPU textures and released 179. A raylib texture has nothing to free it when the managed object is collected, so every window that painted a background or a button face and then closed left it behind -- about half a gigabyte of video memory, after which the driver refuses and refusing kills the process. Windows give their textures back now: 3,298 city windows opened and closed leave 49 textures held, and those are shared art that does not grow.

Civilization II's own saved games load here, so the same position can be opened in both and the numbers set side by side. Doing that found three things. Every city in a loaded game had three trade routes it never had, because an unused route slot was being read as a route to whichever city came first -- worth 120 trade to a city whose squares produced three. Every civilisation was under the wrong flag, because a save stores the tribe as a position in Civ II's leaders table and this game's table is alphabetical: a Celtic game reported itself as Persian and its German rivals as Babylonian. And a city taken from you never changed colour on your map, because losing it is exactly what stops you being able to see it.

With those fixed, Cardiff at 2500 BC and again at A.D. 1240 agrees with the original on size, food produced and eaten, surplus, shields, support, production, trade, corruption, tax and science. Every number the city screen states.

Two rules corrected against Civ II's documentation. Bribing a unit does not cost the Diplomat its life -- that is the one mission either a Diplomat or a Spy walks away from, and it was being spent as though it had incited a revolt. Settlers and Engineers cannot fortify, and were taking the same half-again defence as a Phalanx on top of the twenty hit points they already have.

The game no longer announces every unit a city finishes. Civ II announces buildings and units that cannot fight, and says nothing about a warrior or a horseman; this had it the other way round, so a city in production interrupted the game every few turns.

The City Resources panel reads as four accounts: a coloured band for each of food, trade, the rates and shields, lit from the top, with the food store and the shield box as ramps rather than flat colour.

And the desktop archives carry a note saying to extract the folder before running. A tester reported "Could not load file or assembly System.Runtime", which is what Windows produces when the executable is run from inside the zip -- a correct download failing in a way that reads like a broken one.
The map, under the hands.

Zoom moves in even steps. The scale was linear in (8 + zoom) / 8, which made one step of the wheel double the map at the far end and change it by two and a half per cent up close -- a factor of nearly forty between the largest step and the smallest, so zoomed out it leapt and zoomed in the wheel appeared to do nothing. Every step is nine per cent now, and eight of them double the scale.

Zoom also goes towards the pointer: the point of the map under the cursor is put back under the cursor after the step, rather than the view staying centred on the active unit while the square you were aiming at slid away.

The weird diamond shadows are gone. Every square on the frontier of the explored map was given a softening where it meets the unknown, using a 32x16 checkerboard drawn when Civ II's squares were 64x32. Terrain composes at several times that now, so the mask was stretched until each of its pixels was a block -- and what was a shade became a coarse dark patch over a quarter of the square, on every square along the edge of the black. The city window showed them too, because the edge of a city's radius is a frontier as well.

The marker on a grassland square that yields an extra shield is an eighth of the square rather than a quarter, so it reads as a token on the ground instead of a stone medallion lying in the middle of a field.
Saved games that can be loaded again, and cities that grow.

Saving worked and loading did not. The save writer asked .NET for each field's type, and a field that holds "a value, or nothing at all" answered "object" -- so a research goal was written as an empty object rather than a number. A research goal is set the first time you answer the research prompt, so in practice every real saved game was written unreadable: saving reported success and the game would not open the file again. Anarchy turns and a city's stolen technology went the same way. Saves already on disk open now rather than being lost.

Cities grow. A citizen is only put to work on a square its civilisation can see, and founding a city revealed nothing at all -- so a new city worked its own centre square and nothing else: two food produced, two food eaten, no surplus, and no growth ever. A save from AD 1220 held thirty-four cities across the whole world and the largest was size four.

Clicking away to another window and clicking back stopped units being selectable. Whether a click could begin on a control was decided once, when the pointer entered it, and entering with a button already down -- which is what the click that raises the window looks like -- left it refusing clicks with nothing to re-arm it.

Winning and losing end the game. A player whose last city fell was told their civilisation had passed into memory and then left sitting in a game they no longer had a civilisation in, with no turn ever coming round to them again.
Ctrl and the wheel zoom towards whatever the pointer is over, rather than leaving the view centred on the active unit while the square you were aiming at slid away from the cursor.

A city says everything it has to say at once: order restored and a new unit built in the same turn arrive as one message with one Zoom to City to answer, instead of the second arriving after you had already looked at the city.

Barbarians who were not in a village. Every barbarian in the game came out of a goody hut, so a civilisation that had cleared the huts near it was never troubled again and the Barbarity question chose between four levels of something that only happened when you went looking for it. Raiders now appear in somebody's country every so often, more often the higher the setting and never on Villages Only, landing clear of a city and with their moves spent so there is a turn to prepare. The first two dozen turns are left alone.

Three defence rules corrected against Civ II. Digging in was worth nothing to the weakest units in the game: the defence sum is worked out in fractions and was then rounded down to a whole number, so Warriors fortifying went from 1 to 1.5 and back to 1 while the attacker's side of the same sum was never rounded. That is the shape of "barbarian horsemen kill the fortified city warrior every time". City Walls supersede the fortification bonus rather than multiplying with it, and answer land attacks only. A river adds half a step to the terrain adjustment rather than a further quarter on top of it.

Smaller things: city names on the map are sized to be read rather than growing with the zoom until they are wider than the city; the fortification marker in the city window is fitted to the unit; the website states the version it is actually offering; and the packaged build keeps what the runtime prints, so a crash that kills the process before any handler runs leaves something behind.
Whole features that shipped and had never once run.

You can talk to the other civilisations. Contact, cease-fires, peace, alliances, embassies, reputation and attitude were all carried in every saved game and read by nothing, so civilisations met by walking into each other and fought until one of them was gone. The Foreign Ministry (Ctrl+D) opens a parley with anyone you have met: cease-fire, peace, alliance, a declaration of war, a gift of gold or of an advance. Computer civilisations answer on their own terms and come asking for a cease-fire when they are losing, and a Diplomat can at last establish an embassy. Treaties bind them the way Civ II's do — which is to say not reliably: nobody moves against you while they think well of you, and below that they turn on the weak, on anyone whose economy has eclipsed theirs, and on anyone whose own word is worthless. Breaking a treaty costs two black marks that every civilisation who has met you remembers.

Caravans trade. Cities were given commodities to supply and demand, the city window had a line for trade routes that read a literal "+xx", the map drew the routes in gold, and nothing in the game could create one — a caravan reaching a foreign city was refused as a failed attack. A caravan now offers what Civ II offers: open a route, put its cargo into a wonder, or go on to a richer market. Routes earn their cities trade every turn.

Wonders are unique. Nothing stopped two civilisations, or two cities of one civilisation, from each raising the Pyramids. A finished wonder is withdrawn from every build list in the world, whoever was racing for it is told, and Civ II's three notices — begun, a rival nearly finished, finished — all arrive. The Wonders of the World report (F7) used to open a window of blank rows.

Pollution happens. A city works out how much it makes, the improvement exists, settlers can clear it and the messages were written, and nothing ever put a square of it on the map. Global warming follows if it is left, and is off by default in the new Advanced Settings, along with the cheat and editor menus.

Forty-five menu entries were drawn with no command behind them. Build Mines, Build Fortress, Build Airbase, Clear Pollution, Move Pieces, View Pieces, Center View and Activate Unit all work now, and what is genuinely unimplemented is no longer advertised.

The difficulty levels differ. Computer civilisations pay 160% of the listed price on Chieftain down to 80% on Deity, barbarians hit at a quarter strength on Chieftain and half as hard again on Deity, and there is a tutorial on the levels people learn on — starting with how the number pad moves a unit.
Computer civilisations also research now. Without a Lua script to choose for them they researched nothing at all, for the whole game.
The interface, from a full pass over the 0.1.5 report.

Every message the game shows is narrower and taller — they were set to nearly two thirds of the screen, about a hundred and forty characters to a line, and are now set to roughly the measure of a book. Messages also wait their turn: one comes up at a time, nothing arrives over the top of a battle still being played out, and zooming to a city on a disorder report no longer gets the next report dropped on top of the city window.

The Go To dialog can be left again — Cancel was being read as the show-all-cities toggle and reopened the dialog instead of closing it. Find City now takes the map to the city; its Ok did nothing at all. Typing a letter at any list jumps to the next entry under it, and city names in lists are bigger.

Squares on a city's resource map can all be clicked: the click worked out which square you meant with completely different arithmetic from the one that drew it, and squares they disagreed about could not be selected. Taking a city names it and opens it, losing one says so, a city's size beside its name keeps up with what it builds, and a sleeping unit wakes when something hostile steps alongside. An expensive item's production shields fill the box in rows rather than collapsing to a single line.
Combat draws from the game's own seeded generator now, so a battle can be replayed from a saved game's seed. A starving city disbands a settler it supports before it loses a citizen, as Civ II does.

You can change how you are governed. REVOLUTION has been in the Kingdom menu since the menus were written with nothing behind it, so a civilisation was handed Despotism at the start and stayed under it for the whole game however far it researched. A revolution now costs two turns of anarchy, after which your people ask what they are to become, and researching a government offers the revolution there and then.

Diplomats and Spies do something at last. Everything the Diplomat asks to show — the offer to bribe a unit, the price of inciting a city — was missing from the game's text, so nothing was ever shown and the unit stood there having achieved nothing. Investigate City and Steal Technology are new: an agent brings back an account of a rival city, garrison included, or carries out one of its owner's secrets. A city can only be robbed once. A Diplomat does not come home from any of it; a Spy does, having spent a move.
The game answers the keyboard and the mouse again.

One press of End Turn now plays a whole turn. Starting a civilisation's turn handed control back and waited, which is right for you and wrong for everybody else — a computer civilisation has nothing that comes back later to ask it to carry on, so each rival moved a single unit and then held the turn. With eight rivals on the board that meant pressing Enter eight times, into a game that appeared to be ignoring you, before you could move again. Rival civilisations also move their whole armies now, and their fortify and settler orders actually resolve.

Keypresses are no longer lost. Keys were read by asking about every key on the keyboard once a frame, so a key pressed and released during a frame that ran long had already come back up before it was asked about, and the press simply never happened. Redrawing the map is about ten times faster, a redraw happens when it is asked for instead of waiting up to two seconds on the animation clock, and the side panel keeps answering the mouse after it rebuilds itself.

The research chooser has a Goal button: name an advance to work towards and it lists only the research that leads there, or says plainly when nothing you can begin now brings it any nearer. The goal is remembered in saved games and retires itself when it is reached.
Saving, and a turn that ends when you press Enter.

Save Game and Load Game are in the Game menu and work when clicked; before this they were drawn but carried no action, and saving was only reachable by a keyboard shortcut. "Autosave each turn" has been a checkbox for a long time and now actually writes, three rotating slots taken at the start of each turn. Opening the Save dialog could take the game down before it drew, if the leader's name was shorter than two characters.

Ending a turn no longer takes several presses of Enter. It stopped at the first unit that needed a decision and abandoned the rest of the army, so the units behind it were never processed at all -- a unit told to fortify did not become fortified until whatever preceded it had been dealt with.
Diplomats can buy units and cities. A lone unit in the open can be bribed, a garrison comes with the city it defends, and a capital cannot be bought at any price.

Huts use the original game's measured odds: five outcomes at one chance in five each, with no empty village among them. The coastline is dark water meeting a thread of beach instead of a lit turquoise outline, the generation matte is gone from the citizens and the city roofs, production shields are drawn as an even block, and the marker for a unit killed in combat appears -- it never once did.
The map, from a full beta test.

Roads and railways now meet at the edges of a square instead of scattering as dashes across it, and rivers run as rivers: the sixteen river tiles are drawn to match which neighbours the water actually reaches, and a river arriving at the coast opens into a mouth instead of stopping. An ocean square is drawn as water whatever surrounds it, so a one-square bay is no longer a meadow with whales breaching out of it. Irrigation and farmland are ploughed fields rather than a blue lattice, and the goody hut, the flag over a city and the resource icons are all drawn from the high-resolution art set.

A road is worth a third of a movement point to every unit again, not only to those with more than one point to spend — settlers, warriors and musketeers were walking their own roads at one square a turn. Pressing Enter ends a turn, and the side panel says when the game is waiting for it. When a unit is killed the map holds on the square long enough to see it happen, and marks it. Huts hold something worth finding far more often than they hold nothing, a new city starts building something it can actually build, and the map no longer scrolls off to watch movement the player is not entitled to see.
Fixes a crash introduced in 0.1.1.

Founding a city could leave the game with no unit to move, and asking for the next one then recursed until the process died. It left no crash report, because the failure was a stack overflow, which cannot be caught. Anyone on 0.1.1 should update.
Fixes two crashes and a round of interface problems reported against 0.1.0.

Saving failed permanently once the barbarians had taken a city, and researching an advance that enabled a terrain improvement took the game down. Units and improvements in the Change Production list are drawn at a readable size instead of a few pixels, and the list keeps a stable order so something unlocked by a new advance appears where you would look for it rather than at the bottom. A unit that has finished its turn stops blinking, a unit that slept to heal wakes when it is whole, and disbanding a unit clears it from the city window at once. The city window is finished in the same painted stone as the rest of the interface.
The first release built for Linux, Windows and macOS together, and the first that is not a beta.

Roads and railways are painted art rather than drawn lines, and connect correctly to each of a tile's eight neighbours. The city window is finished in the same stone as the rest of the interface instead of flat grey. The project has been separated from its upstream fork: the solution, the projects, the engine namespace and the save directory all carry the rhYciv name, and saves written by earlier builds are migrated on first launch. Every change is now checked by continuous integration on all three platforms.
